title: The Hidden Language of Cross-Species Cooperation
summary: In the animal kingdom, cooperation isn't limited to members of the same species. A groundbreaking review published in Animal Behaviour shows that communication plays a crucial role in helping different species work together. Led by Dr. Katie Dunkley at the University of Oxford, an international team examined how animals use calls, body movements, visual displays, and other signals to synchronize behavior and maintain mutually beneficial partnerships. One striking example is the greater honeyguide (Indicator indicator), which uses specialized calls to attract humans and lead them to bees' nests. The bird also responds to human calls, creating a two-way dialogue. In Mozambique, fishermen and dolphins have developed a similar partnership: dolphins signal when to cast nets, though the cues vary by region. Cleaner fish like Labroides dimidiatus perform distinctive dances and display bright colors to signal their role to predatory clients, allowing them to safely remove parasites. Even insects get in on the act — lycaenid butterfly larvae use chemical and vibrational signals to recruit ants as bodyguards. The review emphasizes that communication helps manage risk. Signals allow animals to identify trustworthy partners and avoid exploitation. For instance, cleaner shrimp use specific movements to reassure larger fish that they won't be eaten. The researchers also explored how these interspecies signals evolve. Many likely began as simple cues — traits that influence another animal's behavior without originally being meant as communication. Over generations, they become more specialized. Others may have been repurposed from behaviors used in parenting or conflict resolution. "Studying how information flows between species gives us a powerful window into how communication systems originate, change and sometimes coevolve," says Dunkley. The findings challenge scientists to look beyond visual signals and consider multisensory communication, as many species rely on chemical or vibrational cues that are easy to miss. This research not only deepens our understanding of animal behavior but also offers insights into the very roots of language.
why_it_matters: Understanding how animals from different species communicate and cooperate challenges our assumptions about language and intelligence, and could inspire new approaches to collaboration in human society, from diplomacy to AI design.

background_read: Interspecies cooperation, known as mutualism, is a well-documented phenomenon in biology—examples include bees pollinating flowers and oxpeckers cleaning large mammals.

The greater honeyguide (Indicator indicator) has been guiding human honey-hunters in sub-Saharan Africa for centuries, and indigenous communities like the Yao in Mozambique have developed specific calls to communicate with this bird.

Similarly, cooperative fishing between humans and dolphins has been observed not only in Mozambique but also in Brazil and Myanmar, suggesting that such partnerships can arise independently when both sides benefit.
Game theory, a branch of mathematics, helps scientists model how trust and signaling evolve in these partnerships.

Dr. Katie Dunkley's review, published in Animal Behaviour, synthesizes decades of observations to understand the hidden language of cooperation; the University of Oxford, where she works, is one of the world's oldest universities (founded in the 11th century) and a leader in biological research.

The journal Animal Behaviour, established in 1953, is a premier outlet for ethology, and Dunkley's work challenges traditional boundaries between human and animal communication, suggesting that the roots of language might be found in these ancient alliances.

perspectives.description: These partnerships show that cooperation can evolve across species lines, creating remarkable relationships that benefit all participants and revealing nature's ingenuity.

Many of these cooperative systems are threatened by habitat destruction and climate change. For instance, overfishing can break the dolphin-fisherman bond, and deforestation disrupts honeyguide-human partnerships, leading to loss of cultural and ecological heritage.

The review highlights that communication often starts as simple, unintentional cues that gradually become specialized signals. This gradual process helps scientists understand how even rudimentary interactions can, over generations, evolve into complex languages.

Future studies might combine acoustic, chemical, and vibrational sensors to uncover hidden communication networks, which could lead to conservation strategies that protect not just species but their collaborative relationships.
